sources.title: Hans Kelsen (Q84165), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-30): label 'Hans Kelsen', description 'Austrian lawyer (1881-1973)', born 1881-10-11, died 1973-04-19 (also 1973-04-20), citizenship values Austria, United States and others, Korean label present, two images. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Robert Walter, 'Kelsen, Hans', Neue Deutsche Biographie 11 (1977), pp. 479-480 (Bavarian Academy of Sciences, via Deutsche Biographie), read in full in German. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: his Hauptprobleme der Staatsrechtslehre (1911) founding the 'Pure Theory of Law', a critical legal positivism built on the Grundnorm as an assumption, his repeated critical work against natural-law theories, the Vienna School of legal theory, his 1918-20 work on the Austrian federal constitution and its constitutional court, his judgeship there until 1929, posts in Cologne, Prague and Geneva, emigration to the United States in 1940 and Harvard and Berkeley, over 600 writings translated into 24 languages. The author, Robert Walter, is listed in the entry's own bibliography as a co-editor of Kelsen's 90th-birthday Festschrift, so he was close to Kelsen and the entry is admiring (it says his influence on twentieth-century legal science is 'surpassed by no one'); its dates for Cologne and Prague differ from other sources.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hans Kelsen' (print version of the revised article, updated April 2026), read in full: Austrian-American legal philosopher who formulated the 'pure theory' of law, first presented in Hauptprobleme der Staatsrechtslehre (1911); professor at Vienna, Cologne, Geneva and Prague; wrote the Austrian constitution adopted in 1920 and served as judge of the Constitutional Court (1920-30); emigrated to the United States in 1940 and taught at Harvard, Berkeley and the Naval War College; later books include General Theory of Law and State (1945) and The Law of the United Nations. Short encyclopedia entry; it says he 'wrote' the constitution, which other sources qualify as drafting and technical work for a collective project.

Wien Geschichte Wiki (City of Vienna), 'Hans Kelsen', read in full (structured data page based on Czeike's Historisches Lexikon Wien): career chronology including the Exportakademie lecturer 1910-17, the State Chancellery 1918-21, dean of the Vienna law faculty 1920-21, member of the Constitutional Court 1919 to 1930, Vienna chair 1919-29, Cologne 1929-33, Geneva, German University in Prague 1936-38, Harvard 1941-42, Berkeley 1942-52 and the Naval War College 1953-54, and the legacy held at the Hans Kelsen Institute. Municipal reference database; dates for the court tenure and Cologne differ from Britannica and the NDB.

Sara Lagi, 'Hans Kelsen and the Austrian Constitutional Court (1918-1929)', Co-herencia 9 (16), 2012, pp. 273-295 (Universidad EAFIT, via Redalyc), read in the sections on the drafting of the constitution and on constitutional justice: Karl Renner entrusted Kelsen in 1919 with several constitutional blueprints (the first, K-I, favouring the Laender), he was appointed constitutional court judge in 1920 in place of Edmund Bernatzik and remained until 1929, his model of constitutional jurisdiction differed from that of his teacher Georg Jellinek, his 1928 essay on constitutional justice argued that the court should protect minorities and preserve the division of powers, the 1927-29 conservative offensive and the marriage-dispensation dispute that led to the court's reorganisation, and a footnote on his debate with Carl Schmitt over who should guard the constitution. Independent academic article by an intellectual historian; critical of neither side but political-historical in aim, and the final sections on the 1929 amendment and the court's decline were not read.

New World Encyclopedia, 'Hans Kelsen', read in the biography section (about 17,000 characters): his 1905 conversion and the Jewish ancestry that, it says, obliged him to move several times, his 1911 habilitation and Hauptprobleme, his founding of the Austrian Journal of Public Law in 1914, the 1919 request to draft the constitution, the loss of his court seat in 1930 after the marriage-dispensation rulings, Cologne, his dismissal in 1933 when the Nazis took power, Geneva and Prague, the 1940 move to the United States at nearly sixty with only basic English, and the Law of the United Nations. Edited encyclopedia article; narrative is unfootnoted, and its figure of 'almost four hundred' works conflicts with the NDB's 'over 600'.

Austrian National Library, Bildarchiv Austria, portrait photograph 'Hans Kelsen' by Georg Fayer (1892-1950), about 1930, inventory number Pf 6505 C(3), image ID 8026867: the catalogue record states title, persons and date 'um 1930' but no rights statement; checked for the portrait only and not used for scoring.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_kelsen_ndb, src_kelsen_britannica, src_kelsen_lagi | 1911-1960 | national biography + encyclopedia + academic article] Walter describes a critical legal positivism that separates the legal description of norms from sociology and politics, and a lifelong effort to develop the theory, including repeated critical analysis of natural-law doctrines that he found to rely on empty formulas or to derive an 'ought' from an 'is'; Britannica says he required a theory of law to be logically self-supporting; Lagi shows the same method in his 1928 essay on constitutional justice, which works through the subject, criteria and procedure of constitutional review. The sources are scholarly summaries rather than quotations of his reasoning and Walter was a close associate, but three independent descriptions agree on the method.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_kelsen_lagi, src_kelsen_ndb, src_kelsen_nwe | 1920-1931 | academic article + national biography + encyclopedia] Lagi reports that his model of constitutional jurisdiction differed from that of his own teacher Jellinek and that, in the debate with Carl Schmitt, he argued against entrusting the constitution's protection to the president or to a non-judge; Walter records his repeated critique of natural-law theories; New World Encyclopedia says he published a reply to Schmitt in 1931. Schmitt's side of the exchange was not read, and Lagi mentions the debate only in a footnote, so the row is moderate.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_kelsen_ndb, src_kelsen_britannica, src_kelsen_lagi | 1911-1934 | national biography + encyclopedia + academic article] Britannica says he formulated the 'pure theory' of law and Walter says he founded it in the 1911 Hauptprobleme and built a Vienna School around it; Lagi describes his constitutional-court model as distinct from the Jellinek model and as the core of his contribution to the Austrian court. The strongest praise (influence 'surpassed by no one') is Walter's, a close associate's, and the sources do not weigh rival theories, so originality is recorded as high but not at the top. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 76 / 0.60 to 72 / 0.54 because the most superlative support is a close associate's retrospective praise in the NDB and Lagi supports only the court model.

persistence.rationale: [src_kelsen_ndb, src_kelsen_wgw, src_kelsen_nwe | 1930-1960 | national biography + municipal database + encyclopedia] The career chronology shows him continuing to teach and publish after leaving Vienna and Cologne, in Geneva and Prague and from 1940 in the United States, where the NWE says he began with basic English at almost sixty, and Walter says he worked on developing the Pure Theory throughout his life, issuing a second edition in 1960 and a stream of works translated into 24 languages. The row scores sustained scholarly output across moves only; the reasons for the moves and any inference from them are context and are not scored.

adaptability.rationale: [src_kelsen_wgw, src_kelsen_britannica, src_kelsen_nwe | 1929-1954 | municipal database + encyclopedia + edited encyclopedia] He held posts in five countries and several languages: Vienna, Cologne, Geneva, Prague, then Harvard, Berkeley and the Naval War College, and Britannica lists General Theory of Law and State (1945) and The Law of the United Nations among the later books; NWE says he had to teach in a foreign language in Geneva and began English late. The sources give the posts, not how he adjusted, and dates differ between them, so the row is modest.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_kelsen_ndb, src_kelsen_nwe, src_kelsen_britannica | 1905-1952 | national biography + encyclopedia] Walter says that beyond the theory of law he wrote on international law, on the law of the United Nations, on the boundary between nature and society and on the theory of democracy; NWE notes a first book on Dante's theory of the state in 1905, studies of constitutional, administrative and international law, and a founding editorship of a public-law journal. Most of this range is within legal science broadly, so it is rated as moderate.

portrait.reason: No portrait with a rights basis established to the required standard. Rejected: Wikidata image 'Hans Kelsen (Nr. 17) - Bust in the Arkadenhof, University of Vienna', a photograph of a modern bronze bust, which is a derivative of the sculptor's work and has no stated sculptor terms. Best candidate: 'Hans Kelsen (1881-1973) ~1930' by Georg Fayer (1892-1950) from the Austrian National Library (inventory Pf 6505 C(3), image ID 8026867), 789 x 1109 pixels on Commons, tagged 'public domain, author died more than 70 years ago' on Commons and repeated as 'gemeinfrei' on a University of Vienna history page that cites the Commons file itself. Blocker: that is a jurisdiction-only (Austrian life-plus-70) claim; the Austrian National Library record gives only the title, persons and date 'um 1930' and no rights statement, and the date is approximate with no publication date or place. Because Austria protected works for life plus 70 years in 1996, US copyright was restored to published works and would last 95 years from first publication, so the work is public domain in the United States only if it was first published in 1930 or earlier or never published, which no source states. Next step: obtain the Austrian National Library's written reuse terms for image 8026867, or evidence of first publication in or before 1930, or a different photograph with a documented US basis (for example a pre-1931 published photograph or a Berkeley or Bancroft Library item with stated terms). Kind, if resolved: likeness.
